The incident occurred at 1.30am on Wednesday morning. A van carrying a group of men was seen driving past the RUC station. The men opened fire on the van, injuring two of the soldiers. The other two soldiers were injured by flying glass. The incident was reported to the police, but the incident was not reported until 2.45am. The IRA claimed responsibility for the incident, saying the van was carrying people who had been involved in previous terrorist attacks. eval_texts: The case was brought before the Court on [DATE_TIME] by the European Commission of Human Rights. The purpose of the request and the application was to obtain a decision as to whether or not the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Articles 8 and 13 (art. 8, art. 13) of the Convention. The Chamber of seven judges to be constituted included, as ex officio members, Sir [PERSON], the elected judge of [NRP] nationality and Mr. [Person], the President of the Court (Rule 21 § 3 (b) (Art 21 § 4) The hearing was held in public at [LOCATION], [ LOCATION], on the appointed day. On [DATE_TIME], the Delegate of the Commission had notified the Registrar that he did not wish to present any comments in writing. Shortly thereafter, Mr. [PERSON], being prevented from taking further part in the consideration of the case, was replaced as President of the Chamber by the Vice-President of the Court (Rule 21 § 5). The hearing was adjourned until the next day (Rule 38) (art. art. 43) The Government made comments on the application of Article 50 of the Convention. The Court heard addresses by Mr. [Person] for the Government, by Sir [PERSON] for. the Commission and by. Mr.  for the applicants, as well as their replies to its questions. Following deliberations held on [DATE_TIME], the Chamber, by unanimous decision, relinquished jurisdiction in favour of the plenary Court (Rule 50). Having taken note of the agreement of the Agent of the Government and the concurring opinion of the Delegate of the Commission, the Court decided that the consideration of the case should continue without resumption of the oral proceedings (Rule 26) The case was heard by the Honourable Court of Appeal. The applicants’ complaints to the Commission in so far as relevant to the present proceedings all related to the period when Mr. [PERSON] was subject to the ordinary prison regime at [LOCATION]. The facts surrounding those grievances are briefly set out in the following paragraphs. In [DATE_TIME] he was transferred to a Training for Freedom Hostel within the prison (see paragraph 33 below). He was released on [Dates_TIME]. He was in the lowest security category (Category D) from [D dates_TIME) until his release. In the relevant period the normal rules regarding the sending and payment of correspondence were applied to him. The postage of only one three-page letter was paid for out of public funds. Mr. [PERSON]’s incoming and outgoing mail was controlled by the prison authorities in accordance with the normal practice followed at the prison. The applicants asserted before the Commission that on occasions the prison censorship officer read out aloud in front of other inmates letters from Mrs. [HEWITT] laughing or making comments about their contents. The Government have subsequently acknowledged that in fact this rule was applied in error, since the letter in question was addressed to a person connected with the public media, it was a personal one which Mr. [SIXTEEN) should have been allowed to send. The application was rejected on the basis that there was a general prohibition of the passing on by a prisoner of material intended for publication or for use on wireless or television (see paragraph 25 below). Mr. [PERSON] was sentenced to life imprisonment for murder in [DATE_TIME]. He served his sentence in [Person] and Perth Prisons until [Date_TIME], when he was detained as a Category D prisoner (that is, the lowest security category) at [LOCATION]. He was moved to the Training for Freedom Host. He was given a special licence to do unescorted community work outside the prison. He also received special escorted leave and visited his home on two occasions, albeit under the constant supervision of an officer in accordance with the scheme (see paragraph 28 below). He also complained through his Member of Parliament to the Parliamentary Commissioner for Administration (the Ombudsman) The first-named applicant's father was seriously ill and unable to walk or travel. He had requested to serve the latter part of his sentence in [LOCATION] rather than Penninghame Open Prison. He petitioned the Secretary of State for [ LOCATION] on [DATE_TIME] requesting a home visit to his father. The petition indicated that his father had been “ill for a considerable period’, but not that he was dangerously ill, which would have made him eligible for compassionate leave. His request was therefore refused. The decision recommended him to make the effort to get a member of staff to take him out of prison under the special escorted leave scheme. It is necessary, to prevent abuse of the arrangements, to maintain a strict and entirely consistent approach to applications for compassionate visits from all prisoners. The fact that a prisoner is being released for educational or other purposes does not affect consideration of the merits of his application or remove the need for the normal criteria to be met. Mr. [PERSON] is expected to transfer to the formal Training for Freedom (TFF) in [DATE_TIME]. Prior to that he will have a [Date_TIME] home leave and while on TFF he may spend at home. I feel that it would be quite wrong, before that stage is reached, to make a special exception in Mr. (PERSON)’s case and circumvent the rules in relation to either a compassionate visit or a special escorted leave.
